one_liner: Teaching idiom: replace a dynamic_cast type test with a virtual member call; book example code, not a library.
what_it_does: Chapter01/02_dynamic_cast.C is a 50-line Google Benchmark program that times two ways of acting on a Base* pointing at a Derived: calling the virtual f() 64 times per iteration (BM_virtual) and running dynamic_cast<Derived*> 64 times per iteration (BM_dynamic_cast). The lesson is a design rule: when code asks 'is this a Derived?' only to choose behaviour, move that behaviour into a virtual member and let the vtable choose. There is nothing to link against; you apply the pattern to your own hierarchy.
how_it_is_fast: A virtual call loads the vtable pointer, loads the function slot and makes an indirect call; with a single target, as in this benchmark, the indirect branch is always predicted. dynamic_cast instead calls into the C++ ABI runtime (libsupc++ or libc++abi with GCC/Clang, the MSVC runtime), which reads the object's RTTI through the vtable and compares type information before returning the adjusted pointer, so even this best case (one-level hierarchy, cast always succeeds) pays a library call plus type checks.
when_to_use: You own the class hierarchy and hot code branches on dynamic_cast<Derived*>(p) != nullptr to pick behaviour: add a virtual hook in the base and call it instead.

Loops over heterogeneous object collections that type-test every element before processing; the book figures relayed in the record put the virtual call near 1 ns against 5-10 ns for the cast (about 5-10x, derived).
Code that would like to build with RTTI disabled (-fno-rtti): virtual dispatch needs no RTTI, a downcasting dynamic_cast does.
Reviewing hot paths: a quick rule of thumb that an RTTI type test costs several virtual calls, before deciding whether CRTP or std::variant is worth the refactor.
when_not_to_use: The base class is not yours (third-party or frozen ABI): dynamic_cast, or a visitor, stays the tool.
The operation does not belong in the base interface: adding one virtual per caller-specific question bloats the base and couples it to every client.

Cross-casts between sibling bases, casts through virtual inheritance or checks that must fail cleanly with nullptr: the idiom does not answer 'what type is this', and the benchmark covers none of these cases.

Expecting the 5-10x figure on your code: the benchmark uses the cheapest dynamic_cast (one level, always succeeds, since rand() is never seeded and returns non-zero first), and real cost depends on hierarchy depth, multiple inheritance, failing casts and the ABI runtime.
The dispatch itself is the bottleneck and the concrete type is known at compile time: CRTP or std::variant removes the indirect call too (see the sibling CRTP entry).

integration.dependencies: none for the idiom; the benchmark file needs Google Benchmark (not vendored, version not stated)
integration.min_toolchain: any C++11 compiler for the idiom (the file uses override and std::unique_ptr); the repo ships no build files and the README names only GCC, Clang or Visual Studio
integration.platforms: any; README lists Windows, Mac OS X and Linux
integration.thread_safety: not applicable to the idiom; the benchmark is single-threaded

gotchas: Asymmetric harness: BM_dynamic_cast passes every cast result through benchmark::DoNotOptimize, but BM_virtual never observes p->f()'s return value or the member it changes (no DoNotOptimize or ClobberMemory, and the object is deleted after the loop), so a compiler that speculatively devirtualizes and inlines Derived::f can fold the 64 calls; inspect the disassembly before trusting the virtual row.

The rows do different work: the virtual row runs a loop-carried --i on a heap member (a read-modify-write chain through memory when f is really called), the cast row a side-effect-free type test, so the ratio compares idioms rather than equivalent operations.

Google Benchmark's time column is per iteration and each iteration does 64 operations; the repo does not say whether the book's 1 ns and 5-10 ns are per operation or per iteration, so compare the items_per_second column (set by SetItemsProcessed(64*iterations)) when rerunning.

No CMakeLists.txt or Makefile exists for Chapter01, so optimisation level, compiler and Google Benchmark version are up to you; the .C extension is C++ to GCC and Clang, but tools that ignore case may compile it as C (MSVC needs /TP).
pick_this_over_siblings_when: The CRTP siblings (the same book's chapter 8 entry and Eli Bendersky's benchmark) remove the virtual call itself and need the concrete type at compile time; this entry is the step before that, replacing an RTTI type test with a virtual call when the set of derived types is only known at run time.
verified_claims_summary: The book, as relayed by the seed lead and not shown anywhere in the repository, reports about 1 ns for the virtual call against 5-10 ns for dynamic_cast<Derived*> on a one-level hierarchy (about 5-10x, derived), noting that absolute numbers depend on hardware. The repo holds only the Google Benchmark source; compiler, flags, ABI runtime and CPU are not stated, so the result is first-party (tier C) and the virtual row may be inflated by devirtualization.
